question: Can equality gaps derived from Cauchy–Schwarz provide simple differentiable, automatically scaled regularizers for discrete vectors, eigenvectors, and equal-norm orthogonal matrices?

key_findings.claim: The central Cauchy–Schwarz construction is correct and useful: its Gram-determinant gap is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when two chosen vector-valued maps are linearly dependent, while the least-squares identity eliminates an explicit scale parameter.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 1 defines l(x)=||g(x)||²||h(x)||²-|<g(x),h(x)>|². Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz gives the stated zero set, including cases where either map is zero. Lemma 1 rewrites the gap as one map's squared norm times a scalar least-squares residual, so the optimal proportionality coefficient is implicit rather than trained separately. This is an elegant reusable design recipe, although it guarantees only the zero set, not useful composite optimization behavior.

key_findings.claim: The three headline scalar polynomial gaps have the advertised binary, one-sided-binary, and ternary zero sets, and avoid an explicit trainable scale, but they are homogeneous rather than scale-invariant and always include the all-zero vector.
key_findings.evidence: The binary gap N sum x_i^4-(sum x_i²)² vanishes when all squared magnitudes agree; the one-sided gap (sum x_i²)(sum x_i^4)-(sum x_i³)² vanishes when nonzero coordinates share one signed value; the ternary gap (sum x_i²)(sum x_i^6)-(sum x_i^4)² vanishes when nonzero magnitudes agree. Their values scale as fourth, sixth, and eighth powers, respectively. Thus global shrinkage can make the penalty arbitrarily small, x=0 is a target, and only Appendix B.5's normalized variants are invariant to scale.

key_findings.claim: The paper's Hölder generalization in Propositions 2 and 3 is false outside the Cauchy–Schwarz case because equality in Hölder does not mean that the two input vectors are linearly dependent.
key_findings.evidence: For conjugate p=3 and q=3/2, take g=(1,2) and h=(1,4). Their inner product is 9, while ||g||_3 ||h||_{3/2}=9, so the proposed gap is zero, yet g and h are not parallel. Hölder equality instead relates powers of coordinate magnitudes with aligned signs. The proof on page 17 repeats the false linear-dependence equality condition, and Proposition 3 inherits it. Appendix experiments use p=q=2, so this theorem failure does not invalidate those numerical cells.

key_findings.claim: The eigenvector regularizer is a scale-weighted squared eigen-residual that accepts every eigenvector and zero; it does not select a particular eigenpair, and the printed general gradient is incorrect.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 13 is ||x||² min_beta ||Cx-beta x||², so any real eigenvector and x=0 are global minima, with no preference for leading, smallest, or otherwise designated eigenvectors. For general C, differentiating Equation 12 gives 2||x||² CᵀCx+2||Cx||²x-2(xᵀCx)(C+Cᵀ)x. Equation 39 omits the required matrix factor in its final term and does not contain the general (C+Cᵀ) form. This matters because the main experiment describes C as i.i.d. Gaussian, not symmetric.

key_findings.claim: The official eigenvector code changes the stated problem by symmetrizing C and then uses the symmetric-matrix gradient; the reported experiment therefore does not validate the nonsymmetric setting described in the paper.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3.2 says C has i.i.d. standard-normal entries, which is generically nonsymmetric and may not even have a full real eigenbasis. The released eigvec_recovery.m instead constructs C=(C_tmp+C_tmpᵀ)/2 and uses the -4(xᵀCx)Cx term appropriate for symmetric C. Symmetry repairs the code's gradient but conflicts with the written data generator and still does not repair Equation 39. The headline recovery probability is consequently evidence for a hidden symmetric special case only.

key_findings.claim: The matrix regularizer correctly penalizes unequal singular values, but its theorem excludes a genuine global minimizer and its published proof contains a rank-invalid implication and an N-versus-K coefficient inconsistency.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 15 applies the binary equal-magnitude gap to K singular values, so l_om=0 for equal singular values, including all singular values zero. Nevertheless Regularizer 5 states XᵀX=alpha I only for alpha>0, excluding X=0 even though the formula and gradient vanish there. In Appendix A.7, Equation 40 uses N where the definition requires K, Equation 41 switches to K, and the proof infers KXᵀX=||X||²I from X(KXᵀX-||X||²I)=0 without first establishing full column rank. An SVD argument can repair the zero-set result with alpha>=0, but the written proof is invalid.

key_findings.claim: The claimed no-spurious-stationary-point proofs for the scalar gaps are incomplete because their two-coordinate subvector argument ignores derivatives' dependence on global moments.
key_findings.evidence: The appendices reduce a stationary full vector to a selected two-dimensional subvector and then invoke the plotted/two-dimensional stationary structure. But each partial derivative contains sums over all coordinates, so stationarity of the full vector does not imply stationarity of the isolated two-entry objective. The binary, one-sided, and ternary claims appear recoverable by a direct global moment argument; this is best treated as a proof gap, not a demonstrated counterexample to the three claims.

key_findings.claim: The equispaced 2^B-level construction states an impossible mixed-zero equality case and therefore does not establish the advertised discrete alphabet.
key_findings.evidence: The proof claims each auxiliary block y_b may independently be zero or have magnitude 2^(b-1) alpha. Yet its equality equation a1 y_{b,n}²=a2 4^(b-1) for every b,n implies that if any coordinate is zero then a2=0, forcing all blocks to zero; otherwise no block can contain zero. The stated independent mixed-zero choices would also create even sums outside the claimed odd, symmetric alphabet. The two-bit experiment initializes/targets nonzero component blocks and does not test this contradiction.

key_findings.claim: The bounded binary variants contain multiple mutually inconsistent formulas and target-set descriptions, so they are not implementable from the specification as printed.
key_findings.evidence: Regularizer 7 is titled symmetric with target {-alpha,+alpha} but is described as one-sided. Equation 53 prints N sum exp(-2x_i²)-(sum exp(-2x_i²))²; the actual Cauchy–Schwarz construction, derivative, and released expression require the second sum to use exp(-x_i²). As printed, the gap does not promote a finite nonzero binary magnitude. Nearby derivations alternate between (1+x)^-2 and (1+x²)^-1, and Appendix B.2.2 mislabels Regularizer 8 as 7. These look like typesetting/editing errors, but together they make the paper-level contract unreliable.

key_findings.claim: Invexity of a standalone regularizer does not imply exact discrete solutions, global convergence, or invexity for the composite task loss plus finite-weight penalty.
key_findings.evidence: The no-spurious property concerns l in isolation. At a desired discrete point x_d, the regularizer gradient is zero, so a finite smooth penalty cannot cancel a generic nonzero task gradient there; exact feasibility is not generally stationary for f+lambda l. The paper correctly concedes that convergence depends on the combined objective, regularizer, and algorithm, and its neural pipeline explicitly applies a separate hard-quantization step after regularized training. Earlier exact-penalty MPEC work proves finite-threshold equivalence under assumptions; no analogous theorem is supplied here.

key_findings.claim: The underdetermined binary-recovery result is helped by an oracle best-of-restarts protocol that cannot be used when the unknown solution is actually unknown.
key_findings.evidence: The paper allows up to ten random initializations for the nonconvex binary gap versus one run of the convex l_infinity baseline and defines success with the known planted x*. The released binary_recovery.m goes further: criterion_rec(x,xstar) controls stopping and retries until the true xstar is found or ten starts are exhausted. No deployable selection rule among restart outputs is reported. The experiment therefore estimates oracle hit probability over ten attempts, not end-to-end recovery performance from only A and b.

anchors.section: Discrete recovery protocol and restart policy

key_findings.claim: The synthetic recovery study is broad in instance count but does not disentangle the proposed geometry from restart budget, ground-truth scale, or baseline optimization quality.
key_findings.evidence: For each M the authors average 1,000 planted N=100 Gaussian systems, which supports precise protocol-conditional curves. But symmetric binary ground truth is fixed at magnitude one, so the auto-scale benefit is not varied; trainable-scale and fixed-scale regularizers in Appendix C.2 use different landscapes/optimization behavior; and only the CS binary arm receives up to ten starts. One-sided and ternary comparisons use l1 because their planted vectors are half sparse, but no discrete-recovery, exact-penalty, proximal-quantization, or compute-matched baseline is included.

key_findings.claim: The orthogonal-matrix and MAX-CUT demonstrations are too lightly specified to substantiate general optimization efficacy.
key_findings.evidence: The orthogonality section states success was always one for square N=K in {10,100} and M/N from 0.1 to 1, but gives no number of trials, tolerance, residual distribution, runtime, or baseline. Square tests also hide the N/K coefficient error in the appendix/released gradient. The MAX-CUT appendix compares only against initialization and known optima, changes lambda by eight orders of magnitude between graph sizes, and acknowledges failure to reach the optimum on larger graphs.

key_findings.claim: The neural-network results show a viable simple quantization recipe, but not a state-of-the-art or controlled comparison.
key_findings.evidence: The method starts from pretrained full-precision ResNet checkpoints, regularizes for 40/400 epochs, hard-quantizes, and trains scales for 20 more epochs while leaving first/last layers full precision. ImageNet top-1 is 62.8 for binary and 65.3 for ternary, 4.9 and 2.8 points below the best listed baselines; CIFAR-10 gaps are 0.9 and 0.2. All competitor accuracies are copied from their papers rather than rerun under matched initialization, augmentation, pretraining cost, and layer exemptions. The reported ten-run standard deviations for the authors' methods are a useful positive reproducibility signal.

key_findings.claim: Claims of no extra storage, favorable runtime, and regularization robustness are not directly established by the reported measurements.
key_findings.evidence: No peak memory, model-file size, inference latency, throughput, energy, or hardware quantization benefit is measured. Table 11 times isolated epoch types, but the actual 40+20 and 400+20 pipelines are not faster than matched total full-precision epochs at the chosen ratios, and no timing variance is reported. Lambda is selected on 10% of training data; the ImageNet binary ablation changes from 51.5 to 62.8 top-1 between lambda=0.1 and 10, contradicting any global reading of insensitivity to factor-ten changes.

method.core_idea: Choose vector-valued maps g and h whose collinearity encodes a desired structure, then use their Cauchy–Schwarz equality gap as a differentiable nonnegative penalty with an implicit best scalar alignment.
method.mechanism: The Gram determinant ||g||²||h||²-|<g,h>|² is zero exactly when g and h are linearly dependent. Polynomial choices produce equal-magnitude or sparse equal-magnitude vector alphabets; g=Cx and h=x produce an eigen-residual; and g=vec(XᵀX), h=vec(I) penalize unequal singular values and nonorthogonality. The authors minimize these gaps under linear constraints with projected FISTA, or add normalized layerwise gaps to a pretrained network loss, then hard-quantize weights and fine-tune only scale and other remaining parameters.
assumptions: The desired structure can be represented faithfully as collinearity of two tractable vector-valued maps.
The zero vector is acceptable or is excluded/pinned by the task loss or constraints.
The task loss and model parameterization prevent global or layerwise shrinkage from evading a homogeneous penalty.
A useful solution of the composite objective is reachable despite nonconvexity and high-order flat/steep polynomial geometry.
No-spurious-stationary behavior of the isolated regularizer remains practically helpful after adding the task loss.
A finite regularization coefficient yields weights close enough to the target alphabet for the separate hard-quantization step.
One scale per output channel or fully connected row is an appropriate quantization granularity.
Pretraining and subsequent scale-only fine-tuning are available and their cost is acceptable.
For eigenvector use, C has relevant real eigenvectors and accepting any eigenvector is sufficient.
For matrix use, equal column norms are desired in addition to pairwise orthogonality.
Restart selection can be implemented without access to a planted solution in real recovery problems.
Numerical ranges are controlled enough that fourth-, sixth-, and eighth-order moments do not overflow, vanish, or make gradients unusable.

techniques.role: Converts a collinearity condition into a nonnegative differentiable penalty.
Eliminates a scalar alignment parameter through the closed-form projection identity.
Uses equality between global coordinate moments to promote binary or ternary magnitudes.
Penalizes the squared component of Cx orthogonal to x without explicitly optimizing an eigenvalue.
Applies the equal-magnitude gap to singular values through XᵀX to promote equal-norm orthogonal columns.
Optimizes regularizers over affine measurement constraints in synthetic recovery experiments.
Uses up to ten random initializations for symmetric binary and eigenvector recovery.
Adds dimension-normalized CS penalties to output-channel or row weight groups.
Maps regularized weights to binary mean-absolute scales or thresholded ternary levels.
Freezes discrete signs/zeros and fine-tunes shared scales plus biases and normalization parameters.
Appendix variant divides by norm products to remove homogeneity at the cost of singular denominators and extra stationary behavior.
Appendix variants replace high-order polynomials with bounded nonlinear maps, though the printed formulas are inconsistent.

evaluations.setting: N=100 symmetric-binary recovery from M=30–90 Gaussian linear measurements over 1,000 planted instances per M
evaluations.metric: Probability that relative l2 error is at most 1e-2
evaluations.result: The CS binary gap is reported above l_infinity minimization at every undersampling ratio, but receives oracle-selected best-of-up-to-ten restarts.
evaluations.baseline: Convex l_infinity minimization by Douglas–Rachford splitting

evaluations.setting: N=100 one-sided-binary and symmetric-ternary recovery from Gaussian linear systems
evaluations.metric: Probability of relative l2 error at most 1e-2 across 1,000 instances per M
evaluations.result: The corresponding CS gaps substantially outperform l1 minimization across reported undersampling ratios using one initialization.
evaluations.baseline: l1 minimization for half-sparse planted vectors

evaluations.setting: Symmetric-binary recovery comparison among fixed-scale, learned-scale, sinusoidal, nonsmooth, scale-invariant, and Hölder/CS variants
evaluations.result: The main polynomial CS binary gap has the strongest reported curve; learned-scale alternatives are competitive in parts of the sweep and all are solver/protocol dependent.
evaluations.baseline: Prior or derived binarizing regularizers summarized in Appendix C.1–C.3

evaluations.setting: Recovery of a randomly selected eigenvector under Gaussian linear measurements
evaluations.result: The CS gap stays above 0.8 and approaches 1 near M/N=0.5, beating a jointly learned-eigenvalue residual; released code symmetrizes C despite the paper's i.i.d.-matrix description.
evaluations.baseline: Minimization of ||Cx-mu x||² with mu as an extra variable

evaluations.setting: Square N=K=10 and 100 matrix recovery under AX=B
evaluations.metric: Whether FISTA output is an orthogonal matrix
evaluations.result: Success is stated to be one over M/N from 0.1 to 1, without trial count, tolerance, error distribution, or comparison method.

evaluations.setting: ResNet-18 ImageNet weight-only binary and ternary quantization from a pretrained checkpoint
evaluations.result: Binary reaches 62.8±0.3 and ternary 65.3±0.2 versus 69.8 full precision; best listed binary and ternary competitors reach 67.7 and 68.1.
evaluations.baseline: Published, not rerun, results for BWN, SQ-BWN/SQ-TWN, HWGQ, PCCN, ProxyBNN, TWN, and QIL

evaluations.setting: ResNet-20 CIFAR-10 weight-only binary and ternary quantization from a pretrained checkpoint
evaluations.result: Binary reaches 90.3±0.2 and ternary 91.0±0.1 versus 92.2 full precision; the best listed methods reach 91.2.
evaluations.baseline: Published results for DoReFa-Net, LQ-Net, DAQ, and LCR-BNN among others

evaluations.setting: Weighted MAX-CUT on small exact-optimum graphs and larger Gset graphs
evaluations.metric: Cut objective after optimizing the binary CS-penalized relaxation
evaluations.result: The method reaches optima on small graphs and improves initialization on larger graphs but does not reach the known large-graph optima; lambda is changed from 1 to 1e-7.

evaluations.setting: Per-epoch training-time comparison on one RTX 3090
evaluations.metric: Seconds per epoch for full-precision, regularized, and quantized-scale training
evaluations.result: Regularized epochs cost 680 versus 660 seconds for ResNet-18 and 5.2 versus 4.1 for ResNet-20; quantized-scale epochs cost 650 and 3.8, but end-to-end pipeline time, variance, inference speed, and memory are not reported.

limitations: Propositions 2 and 3 use a false equality characterization of Hölder's inequality outside p=q=2.
The isolated regularizer's zero set and stationary points do not imply exactness or global convergence for task loss plus finite-weight penalty.
Every headline regularizer accepts the all-zero vector; homogeneous gaps can be suppressed by shrinking scale.
High-degree polynomial moments can create overflow, underflow, flat gradients near zero, and extreme scale sensitivity.
The eigenvector gap accepts every real eigenvector and does not target an eigenvalue or order components.
The paper's general eigenvector gradient is incorrect, while released experiments silently restrict C to be symmetric.
The matrix theorem improperly excludes X=0 and its proof has coefficient and rank-implication errors.
The no-spurious proofs for scalar gaps use an unjustified reduction from global moment equations to two coordinates.
The equispaced and bounded appendix regularizers contain substantive target-set and formula contradictions.
Binary recovery uses ground truth both to measure success and, in released code, to stop/select among restarts.
Orthogonal recovery has no trial count, tolerance, error statistics, rectangular tests, or baseline.
Neural comparisons reuse numbers from unmatched papers and omit pretraining cost, peak memory, compressed size, latency, energy, and hardware deployment.
First and last neural layers remain full precision, limiting whole-model compression claims.
Only ResNet image classification, synthetic recovery, and small optimization demonstrations are studied; transformers and modern low-bit settings are absent.
No ablation separates the contribution of regularization, hard projection, and post-quantization scale tuning.
failure_modes: A scale degree of freedom in the task model can shrink a weight group toward zero and compensate elsewhere, nearly eliminating a homogeneous CS penalty without becoming usefully quantized.
The composite optimizer can stop at a non-discrete stationary point even when the standalone regularizer has no spurious stationary points.
Eighth-order ternary gradients can vanish near zero or explode for large coordinates, making results highly dependent on normalization and learning-rate schedules.
The eigenvector penalty can converge to an unintended eigenvector or to zero because all are equally optimal for the regularizer.
A nonsymmetric matrix with complex eigenpairs violates the implicit real-eigenvector use case and the implemented symmetric gradient.
Equal singular values can be achieved by X=0, so an insufficiently constraining task term can collapse an intended orthogonal matrix.
Best-of-ten recovery can look successful in simulation but offers no way to identify the correct candidate without oracle ground truth.
A lambda that looks robust on CIFAR can be sharply sensitive on ImageNet binary training, causing large accuracy loss after hard quantization.
Weights can cluster near target levels yet still cross the wrong hard-quantization threshold, making proximity histograms an unreliable task metric.
The printed bounded/equispaced formulas can lead an independent implementation to optimize a different zero set than the authors intended.
Copied baseline accuracies can reverse under a matched recipe, architecture exception policy, or pretraining budget.
A zero CS gap certifies only the chosen algebraic relation, not that the resulting structured solution preserves task behavior.
reusable_insights: Design structural penalties by first expressing the target as equality in a well-characterized inequality, then audit every degenerate equality case explicitly.
The Gram-determinant view separates a clean algebraic zero-set certificate from much harder claims about optimization of a composite objective.
Eliminating a nuisance scale analytically can simplify training, but homogeneity, scale invariance, and automatic scale selection are distinct properties that should not be conflated.
For homogeneous neural networks, test regularizers under function-preserving rescalings across adjacent layers to detect penalty evasion.
An exact structural-penalty paper should report both distance to the constraint set and downstream task quality before and after hard projection.
Multi-start experiments need a candidate-selection rule based only on observable quantities, plus compute-matched single-start and best-of-k baselines.
Symbolically differentiate proposed matrix penalties and test gradients against automatic differentiation on symmetric, nonsymmetric, square, and rectangular cases.
Machine-check inequality equality conditions with small explicit counterexamples before generalizing a familiar p=2 construction.
State zero-vector behavior as part of the target set and add normalization or nonzero constraints when collapse is undesirable.
Separate theorem scopes for the regularizer alone, the constrained problem, the penalized composite, and the actual optimizer.
Quantization studies should match initialization, training compute, exempt layers, augmentation, and scale granularity, and measure actual artifact size and inference performance.
Version the paper, equations, and released code together and add executable formula tests so a symmetric special case cannot silently replace a general claim.
open_questions: Can a CS-derived penalty be made coercive or exactly scale-invariant without singular denominators, collapse, or new spurious stationary points?
Under what assumptions on f does a finite lambda make the global or local minima of f+lambda l_CS exactly structured rather than merely close?
Can an augmented-Lagrangian, proximal, or MPEC formulation retain the implicit-scale benefit while providing finite-threshold exactness?
Which of the binary, one-sided, and ternary no-spurious claims admit short correct global-moment proofs, and what are their strict-saddle geometries?
How should Hölder equality be encoded correctly when the desired relation is power-duality rather than ordinary linear dependence?
Can one construct a differentiable eigen-gap that targets the top-k eigenvectors, excludes zero, handles nonsymmetric matrices, and has reliable stochastic gradients?
Does a rectangular orthogonality experiment retain the reported behavior when K<N and the correct K coefficient is used?
How often do neural network rescaling symmetries let adjacent layers evade CS quantization penalties in practice?
Does the method remain competitive on transformers, language models, activation quantization, and 2–4-bit learned grids under matched compute?
What observable criterion can choose among nonconvex recovery restarts without access to the planted solution?
Do CS-regularized weights improve post-training robustness to hard rounding relative to proximal, annealed, and exact-penalty methods at the same accuracy?
Can automated algebra/property tests catch the appendix's exponent, coefficient, target-set, and gradient drift before publication?

competitive_landscape.title: How to Train a Compact Binary Neural Network with High Accuracy?
competitive_landscape.difference: Tang et al. use a polynomial regularizer that attracts weights to fixed binary values during training. The CS paper recovers this family through an augmented map construction and contributes an implicit free scale, but does not compare under a matched training recipe or establish exactness of the composite neural objective.

competitive_landscape.title: Regularized Binary Network Training
competitive_landscape.difference: Darabi et al. attract weights to {-alpha,+alpha} with W-shaped Manhattan and Euclidean penalties while learning alpha per layer or filter. CS analytically eliminates the common scale into a smooth vector-coupled moment polynomial; Darabi supplies a more BNN-specific recipe and ImageNet study but no broad structural construction or no-spurious analysis.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv:1812.11800 version available on checked date

competitive_landscape.title: ProxQuant: Quantized Neural Networks via Proximal Operators
competitive_landscape.relationship: closest established regularized-learning formulation for neural quantization
competitive_landscape.difference: ProxQuant optimizes W-shaped quantization regularizers with proximal updates and analyzes stability relative to straight-through training. CS offers ordinary differentiability and an implicit scale, while ProxQuant has an algorithm designed around the nonsmooth/nonconvex quantization geometry and stronger composite-optimization motivation.

competitive_landscape.title: BinaryRelax: A Relaxation Approach for Training Deep Neural Networks with Quantized Weights
competitive_landscape.relationship: continuous-relaxation predecessor for binary network training
competitive_landscape.difference: BinaryRelax anneals from a continuous relaxation toward quantized weights and is evaluated as an end-to-end training algorithm. CS instead regularizes a pretrained full-precision checkpoint, then applies an explicit hard projection and scale-only tuning. The latter is simpler, but the paper does not control for the different training budgets or initialization regimes.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv:1801.06313 version available on checked date

competitive_landscape.title: An Exact Penalty Method for Binary Optimization Based on MPEC Formulation
competitive_landscape.relationship: stronger exact-penalty theory for binary structure
competitive_landscape.difference: Yuan and Ghanem reformulate binary optimization with complementarity and prove local/global minimizer equivalence after a finite penalty threshold. CS supplies a smoother, scale-adaptive algebraic gap but proves no finite-lambda exactness for f+lambda l; its standalone invexity should not be read as an exact-penalty guarantee.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive Binary-Ternary Quantization
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct binary/ternary regularization competitor with adaptive levels
competitive_landscape.difference: Razani et al. jointly adapt binary-versus-ternary behavior during neural quantization. CS provides a unified moment construction for both alphabets and one implicit scale per group, but evaluates them as separate manually selected regimes and trails stronger published ImageNet results.

competitive_landscape.title: Can We Gain More from Orthogonality Regularizations in Training Deep Networks?
competitive_landscape.difference: Bansal et al. compare Frobenius, spectral, mutual-coherence, and restricted-isometry-inspired penalties for near-orthogonal neural weights and evaluate downstream training. The CS matrix gap uniquely equalizes singular values with an implicit common scale, but tests only affine synthetic recovery and does not benchmark neural orthogonality or rectangular matrices.

competitive_landscape.title: EigenGame: PCA as a Nash Equilibrium
competitive_landscape.difference: EigenGame targets ordered leading eigenvectors through coupled utilities and supplies convergence analysis plus massive-data experiments. The CS eigen-gap is a simpler scalar residual with no explicit eigenvalue, but accepts every eigenvector and zero, provides no target ordering, and its reported implementation silently assumes symmetry.

competitive_landscape.title: Improved Imaging by Invex Regularizers with Global Optima Guarantees
competitive_landscape.relationship: prior applied invex-regularizer framework with composite guarantees
competitive_landscape.difference: Pinilla et al. construct proved invex regularizers for imaging and analyze when complete reconstruction objectives retain global-optimum guarantees. The CS paper proves or claims invexity mainly for isolated gaps and explicitly concedes that the task-plus-regularizer composite may not inherit it.

competitive_landscape.title: Invex Programs: First Order Algorithms and Their Convergence
competitive_landscape.relationship: optimization theory invoked by the paper for invex objectives
competitive_landscape.difference: Barik, Sra, and Honorio develop first-order algorithms under explicit invex-program assumptions. Their results do not automatically apply when an invex CS gap is added to an arbitrary task loss; verifying the complete objective and algorithmic assumptions is still required.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv version available on checked date

competitive_landscape.title: Non-negative Matrix Factorization with Sparseness Constraints
competitive_landscape.relationship: uncited precursor to the normalized norm-ratio geometry
competitive_landscape.difference: Hoyer's scale-invariant l1/l2 sparseness measure uses essentially the same normalized moment geometry that Appendix B.5 applies to one-sided/binary structure. The target application differs, but the resemblance narrows novelty of the normalized variant and suggests importing mature constraint-projection and numerical-stability analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: PARQ: Piecewise-Affine Regularized Quantization
competitive_landscape.relationship: contemporary regularized quantization method with stronger optimization analysis
competitive_landscape.difference: PARQ uses convex piecewise-affine regularization with aggregate proximal stochastic updates, proves last-iterate convergence, interprets STE asymptotically, and evaluates convolutional and transformer vision models. CS is smoother and algebraically versatile, but its quantization theory stops at the isolated zero set and its experiments cover only ResNets with a hard-projection stage.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Cauchy–Schwarz regularizers are a novel, general class of simple differentiable, automatically scaled, often invex penalties that can impose discrete values, eigenvector alignment, and orthogonal-matrix structure and enable competitive large-scale optimization.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper does contribute a clean reusable map-design recipe, three compact scale-adaptive moment gaps, a singular-value interpretation of soft orthogonality, and a straightforward pretrained-network quantization pipeline. However, an explicit Cauchy–Schwarz gap regularizer predates it in imaging; fixed/adaptive binary penalties, proximal/relaxation QAT, exact binary penalties, orthogonality penalties, invex regularization, and scalable eigensolvers are mature fields. The Hölder extension is false, several appendix theorems/formulas conflict, and no exactness or convergence result covers the complete task objective.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Novelty is strong at the level of a memorable unifying algebraic recipe and moderate for the particular implicit-scale polynomial constructions. It is limited as optimization theory or quantization state of the art. The correct core is promising as a library of candidate penalties, but broad claims of generality and reliability need theorem repair, machine-checked specifications, non-oracle evaluation, and matched contemporary baselines.

reviewer_notes: Read all 27 extracted pages, including every main equation, theorem/proof, appendix variant, recovery experiment, quantization table, lambda ablation, runtime table, MAX-CUT example, and loss landscape. Cross-checked the official ICLR/arXiv record, the released CS_regularizers MATLAB/PyTorch code, and twelve primary-source competitors on IEEE/AAAI/SIAM/CVF/NeurIPS/OpenReview/JMLR/PMLR/arXiv records as of 2026-08-23. The explicit Hölder counterexample was recomputed algebraically. General eigen-gradient and matrix-gradient claims were independently differentiated; code was inspected to distinguish paper equations from implemented symmetric special cases and to identify xstar-dependent stopping/restarts. The scalar no-spurious statements are marked as proof gaps rather than false theorems because no counterexample was established. No generated projection was rebuilt.
